title: Greetings and Their Replies
description: Every Egyptian greeting has a fixed reply, and the reply is the lesson. Twelve greetings heard as pairs — morning, evening, peace, how-are-you — until you know what comes back before it is said.
approach: GPA Phase 1 — receptive first. Every greeting is heard as a pair (greeting → reply) with two speakers on screen; the learner taps the reply that fits. Production is optional shadowing at the end.
can_do: Greet someone and answer their greeting
Say good morning, good evening and goodbye
Ask how someone is and say you are fine

grammar.title: -ak or -ik: the ending tells you who you are talking to
grammar.explanation: Listen to the end of إزيك. To a man it is izzayyak; to a woman it becomes izzayyik (often written إزيكي); to a group it is إزيكو. The same little ending sits on أخبارك (akhbaarak / akhbaarik). You do not need to build these yet — just notice that the last vowel changes with the person in front of you, and copy the one you hear.

culture.title: The reply is the lesson
culture.note: Egyptian greetings come in pairs, and the second half is not optional. صباح الخير is answered with صباح النور — or, if the other person likes you, صباح الفل ('morning of jasmine') or صباح القشطة ('morning of cream'): each reply tries to outbid the greeting. السلام عليكم is answered word for word with وعليكم السلام. If someone says أهلاً وسهلاً, answer أهلاً بيك (to a man) or أهلاً بيكي (to a woman). Shake hands with the right hand; between friends of the same gender a kiss on each cheek is normal, but let the Egyptian make that move first.

phrases.english: Morning of jasmine (a warm reply to good morning)
Welcome to you (reply to أهلاً وسهلاً, to a man)
God keep you safe (reply to goodbye)

culture.title: How are you? is asked three ways at once
culture.note: Do not be surprised when an Egyptian fires إزيك؟ عامل إيه؟ أخبارك إيه؟ at you in one breath and moves on before you answer. The questions are the greeting; the answer is always some version of كويس، الحمد لله, and then you throw وإنت؟ back. Use أخبارك إيه with friends and people your age, not with your boss or someone's grandmother — for them, إزيك حضرتك is the safe form.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The all-purpose Egyptian hello, for anyone at any hour — also the reply when someone greets you first. مرحبا is understood but sounds imported; Egyptians say أهلاً.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man in a doorway raising a hand in greeting, smiling, a Cairo street behind him.
vocabulary.video_hint: The first word said when two people meet; street interviews open with it.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The greeting for walking into a room, a shop, a taxi. Slightly more formal than أهلاً and used by Egyptians of every religion. Always gets the fixed reply — never answer it with أهلاً.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man entering a small shop with his right hand raised slightly, the shopkeeper looking up.

example.english: Peace be upon you, sir (to an older man)

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone entering a room or shop; the greeting is the first thing said.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The only correct answer to السلام عليكم. The two halves swap places — hear it as one melody rather than two words. Egyptians often add ورحمة الله.
vocabulary.image_scene: The shopkeeper from the previous card answering with a nod and a hand to the chest.

example.english: And upon you peace — come in

vocabulary.video_hint: The second speaker in any greeting scene; often overlaps the first greeting.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Used until around noon. Note the Egyptian vowel in خير — kheer, not khayr. First meeting with ص: a heavier, darker s that colours the whole word.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman opening balcony shutters onto a bright morning street, waving to a neighbour.
vocabulary.video_hint: Morning-routine vlogs; the first line to camera or to a family member.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The standard reply. Warmer versions — صباح الفل، صباح القشطة — outbid it and are heard all the time. Learn the pattern: reply with a nicer noun than the one you were given.
vocabulary.image_scene: The neighbour from the previous card answering from her own balcony, coffee cup in hand, sun behind her.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any reply to صباح الخير; listen for the alternatives الفل and القشطة.

vocabulary.teaching_note: From the afternoon onwards — in Cairo that starts earlier than you would expect, around three. Reply: مساء النور. The hamza at the end of مساء is barely heard.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two friends meeting outside a café at dusk, neon signs beginning to light up on the street.
vocabulary.video_hint: Evening scenes: arriving at a gathering, the opening of an evening show.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Egyptian how-are-you, unmistakable to any Arab. To a woman: إزيكي (izzayyik); to a group: إزيكو. Never كيف حالك (a textbook), never شلونك (Gulf). The doubled يّ makes it sound Cairene.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two men clasping right hands at a street corner, one leaning in with a broad smile.
vocabulary.video_hint: Two people meeting; the greeting is the first thing said, usually with a handshake.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The default answer to every how-are-you. A woman says كويسة. الحمد لله alone also works and is said whatever the speaker's religiosity. Then return the question with وإنت؟.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman answering with a relaxed smile and a small nod, hand on her chest.
vocabulary.video_hint: The reply in any greeting scene; often the interviewee's first full sentence.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said to a guest, a customer, a new arrival. Reply: أهلاً بيك / بيكي / بيكم. Egyptians also welcome you with نورت ('you've lit the place up'), answered by ده نورك.
vocabulary.image_scene: A host opening an apartment door wide with both arms out in welcome, guests on the landing.
vocabulary.video_hint: A host greeting arrivals at a door; a shopkeeper greeting customers.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said by the person staying to the person leaving, and answered الله يسلمك. Between friends a quick سلام or باي does the same job.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man waving from a doorway as a friend walks away down the street.
vocabulary.video_hint: The end of a visit or a phone call; the sign-off of a vlog.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The friendly Egyptian see-you. To a woman: أشوفكي (ashuufik). Another warm version is أشوفك على خير — 'see you well'. Usually followed by إن شاء الله, which here just means 'hopefully'.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two young women parting on a metro platform, one calling back over her shoulder.
vocabulary.video_hint: Friends parting; the closing seconds of a vlog.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'your news is what?'. Casual, for friends and people your age — not for elders or superiors. To a woman: أخباركِ إيه (akhbaarik). Same answer as إزيك: كويس الحمد لله.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two friends at a café table leaning in over glasses of tea, one gesturing 'so, what's new?'.
vocabulary.video_hint: Friends catching up; usually the second or third question after إزيك.

vocabulary.english: how are you doing? (to a man)
vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'doing what?'. Extremely common alongside إزيك. To a woman: عاملة إيه (ʿamla eeh); to a group: عاملين إيه. Same answer: كويس الحمد لله.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man on the phone smiling, one hand open in a 'so how are you?' gesture.

example.english: How are you, how are you doing?

vocabulary.video_hint: Phone-call openers and street interviews; often chained straight after إزيك.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The polite return of any how-are-you. To a woman: وإنتي (w-enti). Without it the greeting feels unfinished.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman pointing an open palm back at the person who asked, eyebrows raised.
vocabulary.video_hint: The turn-taking moment in a greeting; the second speaker hands the question back.

dialogue.speaker: Mona
dialogue.english: And upon you peace — hi, Karim

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: How are you, Mona? How are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: تمام الحمد لله. يلا، أشوفك بعدين
dialogue.transliteration: tamaam el-ḥamdu lillaah. yalla, ashuufik baʿdeen
dialogue.english: All good, thank God. Right — see you later

sound_spotlight.explanation: Two h-sounds. ه is the ordinary English h of 'hello'. ح is breathier, made by tightening the throat as if fogging a mirror. This lesson has both in its two most repeated words, so you can hear them side by side.
A heavy s made with the tongue pulled back, which darkens the vowel after it: ṣabaaḥ sounds deeper than a plain sabaaḥ. Heard passively here; you will contrast it with س in Lesson 5.
The y in the middle of إزيك is held twice as long — iz-zay-yak. Doubling a consonant is meaningful in Arabic, and this word is the first place you can feel it.

lesson_sequence.detail: A door opening onto a Cairo stairwell. One line of English: greetings in Egypt come in pairs; today you learn twelve and their replies. Tap يلا.
Six greeting → reply pairs, each acted by two speakers on a split card. Native audio auto-plays greeting then reply; Arabic shown, English small underneath. Tap to replay either half.
Audio of a greeting plays; three replies appear as cards; tap the one that fits. Wrong taps replay the correct pair. Covers the six pairs plus أخبارك إيه and أشوفك بعدين.
The full dialogue plays with speakers highlighted line by line. Second pass: the learner taps when a turn changes hands.
Four replies only — وعليكم السلام, صباح النور, كويس الحمد لله, الله يسلمك — played and echoed by the learner with a simple record-and-compare bar. No score.
Twelve items, audio only: hear the greeting, tap the reply; hear the reply, tap the greeting. Missed items replay with both halves.
Words-learned counter rolls to 26. Nudge: say السلام عليكم to the next Arabic speaker you meet and listen for the reply.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you walk into a shop or café run by Arabic speakers, say السلام عليكم and wait. The reply will come back word for word.
real_world_prompts.context: Lesson-complete screen. Lowest-risk production task in the course: a fixed phrase with a fixed reply.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Text an Egyptian friend صباح الخير tomorrow morning and see which reply you get — النور, الفل or القشطة?
real_world_prompts.context: Next-morning notification. Written practice of the reply pattern; primes the learner to notice the outbidding replies.

real_world_prompts.prompt: In your next tutor session, open with إزيك؟ عامل إيه؟ and answer their questions with كويس الحمد لله، وإنت؟
real_world_prompts.context: Tutor prompt. Rehearses the full three-question greeting chain in one turn.

video_needs.scene: Two people greeting each other at a door or on the street, the reply clearly audible; Easy Arabic street-interview intros are ideal.
